summary: Defines how the Service Location Protocol version 2 is used over IPv6 networks. Since SLP relies on UDP and TCP, the changes needed are small.

eli5.summary: A directory that helps you find printers on the old network now also works on the new kind of network, with only a few tweaks.

questions: how does slpv2 work with ipv6
subtitle: The small set of changes that lets Service Location Protocol version 2 find network services over IPv6.

tldr.problem: The Service Location Protocol (SLP) helps computers discover network services without manual configuration, but SLPv2 was written for IPv4, which has broadcast and a single multicast address. IPv6 has neither broadcast nor the same addressing rules.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3111 drops broadcast in favour of multicast, writes IPv6 addresses in service: URLs as bracketed literals, assigns a range of IPv6 multicast group-ids chosen by hashing the service type, and adds scope rules so agents never hand out addresses that the requester cannot reach.
tldr.outcome: SLPv2 works over IPv6 with only minor changes, because it already relies on UDP and TCP. The RFC recommends SLPv2 in general and on IPv6 networks in particular, and does not define SLPv1 over IPv6.

today: RFC 3111 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on SLPv2 as defined in RFC 2608.

sections.title: What Changes for IPv6
sections.content:
The Service Location Protocol (SLP) gives computers a scalable way to discover and select network services, so they need less static configuration. RFC 2608 defines version 2 (SLPv2). RFC 3111 lists what must change to run it over IPv6.

The abstract notes that SLPv2 relies on UDP and TCP, so the changes are minor. There are four: no broadcast requests, a way to write IPv6 addresses in URLs, use of IPv6 multicast addresses and address scopes, and restricted propagation of service advertisements.

The RFC covers only SLPv2. It says there was no implementation or deployment of SLPv1 over IPv6 at the time, and it recommends that SLPv2 be used in general and on networks that support IPv6.
sections.eli5: The directory service already knows how to talk over the network. It only needs a few small tweaks to work on the newer kind of network.

sections.title: No Broadcast, Multicast Instead
sections.content:
Over IPv4, SLP can use broadcast to send request messages. IPv6 uses link-local multicast in place of broadcast, so broadcast-only configuration for SLP is not supported under IPv6.

A User Agent (UA) that wants to discover Directory Agents, or to ask several Service Agents at once, must multicast its request to the appropriate multicast address. This change modifies the requirements in Section 6.1 of RFC 2608.
sections.eli5: On the old network you could shout to the whole room. On the new one you must send your question to a named group instead.

sections.title: IPv6 Addresses in service: URLs
sections.content:
The RFC says to use the DNS name of a service whenever possible. Numerical addresses matter when SLP runs without DNS, for example when a group of systems is connected with no prior configuration of servers.

In that case a numerical IPv6 address in a service: URL is written as a literal inside square brackets, following the format for literal IPv6 addresses in URLs (RFC 2732) and the textual form from RFC 2373.

The RFC gives two examples. A site-local address in a directory agent URL looks like service:directory-agent://[FEC0::323:A3F9:25ff:fe91:109D]. A link-local address for a printer on a network with no routers or DNS looks like service:printer:ipp://[FE80::a15A:93ff:fe5D:B098]:8080/path.
sections.eli5: If you do not have a street name, you can write the house number in brackets. The brackets tell everyone where the number starts and ends.

sections.title: Multicast Group-IDs and the Hash
sections.content:
SLPv2 for IPv4 uses one multicast address, because only 256 relative assignments were available. IPv6 has scoped addresses and room for a range, so SLPv2 for IPv6 uses these group-ids, each combined with the scope prefix FF0X:

  • SVRLOC (FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:0:116) for Service Type Request and Attribute Request messages.
  • SVRLOC-DA (FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:0:123) for multicast Service Requests for service:directory-agent, and for the unsolicited DA Advert messages that Directory Agents send.
  • The Service Location range FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:1:1000 to FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:1:13FF for all other multicast Service Requests.

To pick the group within the range, the Service Type string from the SrvRqst is hashed to a value from 0 to 1023. That value is the offset into the range. SAs join the groups matching the service types they advertise. The hash starts an unsigned 32-bit value at 0, then for each UTF-8 byte multiplies by 33 and adds the byte. The low-order 10 bits of the result are used.

The RFC's worked example: service:service-agent hashes to 0x01d8, so the group is FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:1:11d8.
sections.eli5: Each kind of service gets its own club chat. A little math on the service's name decides which chat it belongs to, so everyone gets the same answer.

sections.title: Scoping Rules for Joining, Sending and Replying
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses and multicast groups come in different scopes. Without rules, an agent could find a service it cannot reach, such as a UA that asks with site-local multicast and gets back a URL holding a link-local address for a service on another link.

Joining. An agent MUST NOT join a multicast group with greater scope than the scope it is configured with for unicast. An interface with only a link-local address joins scopes FF01 and FF02. With a site-local or global address, the scope of joined groups can be no greater than FF05, and SAs and DAs MUST join all scopes FF01 to FF05. A DA MUST join SVRLOC-DA to receive requests for DAAdverts, and a SA MUST join it to receive DAAdvert messages. A SA MUST join the service groups for the services it advertises. It MAY join SVRLOC, which is optional to implement.

Sending. The maximum scope for a multicast SLPv2 message is site-local (FF05). The source address MUST have a scope no less than the scope of the multicast group.

Replying. SAs and DAs MUST work out which scope a service URL address is in, resolving host names if needed. They MUST NOT respond to a SrvRqst with a URL whose address scope is less than the scope of the request's source address.
sections.eli5: You only tell people about places they can actually walk to. If someone asks from far away, you do not give directions that only work inside one building.

sections.title: Agents With Multiple Interfaces
sections.content:
A scope zone is a connected region of topology of a given scope. Two different sites are two different zones of the same scope. A host with several interfaces on different links is attached to several link-local zones. The core rule: an SLPv2 agent MUST NOT propagate service advertisements from one zone to another. Literal-address service locations in SrvReg, SrvRply, AttrRst, SAAdvert or DAAdvert messages MUST only go to agents on the same zone.

The RFC suggests, as a prudent strategy, not issuing messages with link-local service locations except on the interface where the service is known to reside, because it is often hard to tell whether two interfaces share a link.

Multihomed UA. It MUST use active discovery to find DAs and MUST issue requests with increasing multicast scope from FF01 up to FF05. To discover everything it must ask in every zone.

Multihomed SA. It MUST NOT return information about services in a different zone than the request, MUST NOT register a service with a DA in another zone, and MUST NOT put an address into a SAAdvert on a zone where it is not valid. It starts DA discovery at scope FF02 and, with a site-local or global source address, MUST reissue with increasing scope up to FF05, in each zone.

Multihomed DA. It MUST track which interface each registration came from, and keep a registration from being discovered in another zone. It MUST answer active DA discovery with the same scope as the request, and multicast unsolicited DAAdverts on each interface with link-local and site-local source addresses (link-local only if that is all it has). The DA URL MUST contain the address of the greatest scope configured in that zone.
sections.eli5: A person standing in two different rooms must not carry one room's secrets to the other. They tell each room only what belongs to that room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
UAs and DAs MAY ignore all unauthenticated Service Location messages when a valid IPSec association exists. SAs and DAs MUST be able to use the IP Authentication Header and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload for Service Location messages whenever an appropriate Security Association exists.

SLP can also produce digital signatures to verify message contents. The RFC says nothing in these IPv6 modifications weakens or strengthens that technique.
sections.eli5: If you have a secret handshake with someone, you can ignore strangers. The old signature trick still works the same as before.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The range FF05::1:1000 to FF05::1:13FF was already assigned by IANA in RFC 2375 for SLP. This document defines how the wider FF0X::1:1000 to FF0X::1:13FF range is used, and IANA has assigned it for SLP.

The addresses are fully defined here, so no registry is needed for assigning more.
sections.eli5: The group of numbers for these chats was reserved ahead of time, so nobody else will use them.
